title: Fraction Maker
context: Grade 3, the first working topic of the fractions chapter. An adult sees a pizza being sliced and a plate being filled, which a real pizza and a crayon can do. What is being settled is that a fraction needs equal parts, and which of the two written numbers counts what. A child who reads the top and bottom as two ordinary numbers puts the taken count underneath, and a child who thinks any cut gives halves will name unequal parts without a worry.

writeup.why: Cut a real thing into equal parts and name them, take some parts and write the fraction with a top and a bottom number, see that equal top and bottom numbers make one whole, and write a fraction of a group of real things.
writeup.look: A kitchen table with a shelf of wholes along the top, an amber board with the chosen whole and a Cut dial, a deep blue plate beside it, a fraction card and a words card at the right, Put together, Shape view and Group view buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fraction Maker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many parts are taken, out of how many parts there are in all. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A kitchen table fills the working area. A shelf of wholes runs across the top at x 90, y 214, 980 by 76, holding five small real things: a round chapati with toasted spots, a pizza with toppings, a round cake, a chocolate bar with its squares and a jug of juice with equal marks, and a torn roti at its far end. The chosen whole comes down onto an amber board 360 by 320 at x 100, y 306, labelled Left: the chapati, pizza or cake about 300 across, the bar 320 long, the jug 150 wide and 280 tall. Near-black cut lines are drawn before anything is taken. A deep blue plate 300 by 320 at x 490, y 306, labelled Taken, waits beside the board: tapping a part lifts it onto the plate, where it keeps its natural colours and its shape, and tapping it there puts it back. In the plain Shape view the same cut whole is drawn as a flat shape and a part that is taken is deep blue, labelled Coloured. The fraction card stands at x 810, y 306, 290 by 220: a top box, a level line and a bottom box, the top labelled numerator and the bottom labelled denominator once the child has met the words. The words card stands under it at x 810, y 540, 290 by 80, and says the name in writing, such as one-third. The Cut dial stands at x 100, y 650, 300 wide, with the numbers two to ten written on it, and the Uneven cut slider beside it at x 420, y 650, 200 wide. The Put together button stands at x 650, y 640, 160 by 60, the Shape view button at x 830, y 640, 130 by 60 and the Group view button at x 980, y 640, 120 by 60, each labelled in words. When the parts are put together the slices slide off the plate and click one by one back into their places, and the last click closes the pizza box into one whole inside a green outline, labelled Whole. In Group view the board is swapped for a long shelf at x 90, y 300, 1000 by 200, holding up to twenty separate real things, mangoes, laddoos, kites, balloons, bananas or bangles, each 80 across with a clear gap, in rows of ten. Tapping one lifts it into the deep blue basket at x 90, y 530, 400 by 170, labelled Taken, and the things still on the shelf are lit amber and labelled Left. In Group view the fraction card shrinks to 240 by 190 at x 540, y 520, the words card moves to x 810, y 540, and the Cut dial and Put together button fade to half strength. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the top number and then the bottom number into the fraction card. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting it. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, labelled Coloured or Taken, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of the same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket, labelled Left. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, labelled Whole, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring, labelled Bigger. A part of a plain drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its near-black outline, every cut line is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last fraction as a stacked number and in words, with its whole or its group still in the frame beside it.

phases.win: the cuts settle into equal parts and the name card reads one-third on the pizza
phases.does: turns the Cut dial to two on the chapati, three on the pizza and four on the cake, reads the name card, then tries the torn roti
phases.goal: equal parts of one whole have names: two are halves, three are thirds, four are quarters
phases.says: Cut the chapati into equal parts. What is one part called?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a roti is torn into two pieces, one bigger than the other. Can each piece be called a half? Why?
phases.feels: the pieces becoming equal and a name arriving only when they do
phases.hands: Fold a roti or a paper plate pizza into two, three and four parts of the same size, tear one roti on purpose, and say the name of one part aloud each time.
phases.tries: First rung: count the parts aloud. Second rung: check that every part is the same size, laying one on another. Third rung: the same task with two parts only, before three and four return.

wrong.why: half is the first part name a child learns, so it feels like the name for any part
wrong.move: calls every part a half, whatever the number of cuts
wrong.screen: the Cut dial runs from two up to four on the pizza and the cake with the parts counted aloud in amber, and the name card changes its name each time the count changes

wrong.why: the pieces are still parts of the same roti, so a name seems fair
wrong.move: names the pieces of the torn roti
wrong.screen: the name card stays blank and says in words that the pieces are not equal, and the slider slides back so the roti closes into equal parts

phases.screen: a chapati, a pizza and a cake on the shelf with their cuts drawn and nothing taken, and a torn roti at the end
phases.soWhat: equal parts have names: two are halves, three are thirds, four are quarters
phases.concept: Equal parts: halves, thirds and quarters

phases.win: the card shows the stacked fraction and its two boxes light up as numerator and denominator
phases.does: lifts pieces onto the blue plate, or fills the jug mark by mark, then types the taken count above the line and all the parts below it
phases.goal: the bottom number counts all the equal parts and the top number counts the parts taken
phases.says: Take some pieces. Count the pieces you took, then count all the pieces.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a jug of juice has some marks filled. Which number tells how many equal marks the whole jug has?
phases.feels: the card filling from two counts: all the parts below the line, the parts taken above it
phases.hands: Break a chocolate bar or fold a paper bar along its squares, take some pieces, write the number taken on a card, then write the number of all the pieces under it.
phases.tries: First rung: count all the parts, taken or not. Second rung: count the parts on the blue plate only. Third rung: the same task with just one part taken, before more are taken.

wrong.why: the bigger number looks as if it belongs on top
wrong.move: types the taken count at the bottom and the count of all the parts on top
wrong.screen: the card turns the numbers round once, and the parts are counted in amber: first all of them, which light the bottom box, then the taken ones on the blue plate, which light the top box

wrong.why: the parts on the board are just as easy to count
wrong.move: counts the parts left on the board as the top number

phases.screen: a chocolate bar, a jug of juice and a pizza on the shelf, the blue plate empty, and a card with a line and two empty boxes
phases.soWhat: the bottom number counts all the equal parts and the top number counts the parts taken
phases.concept: Coloured parts: the top and bottom numbers

phases.win: the last slice clicks in, the pizza closes inside the green outline and the card shows the same number twice
phases.does: puts the slices back into the box one by one, or taps Put together, and types the missing top or bottom number
phases.goal: when the top and bottom numbers are the same, every part is taken and together they make one whole
phases.says: Put the slices back in the box. What do they make?
phases.check: Away from the screen: you eat all four quarters of a chapati. How many chapatis have you eaten? What is the top number and what is the bottom number?
phases.feels: the slices clicking back one by one until the pizza closes with no gap
phases.hands: Cut a paper plate pizza into equal slices, take every slice, then lay the slices back together into one circle and write the fraction. Then hide one slice and ask how many are missing.
phases.tries: First rung: count all the slices below the line. Second rung: count the slices in the box above it. Third rung: the same task with only two slices, before more slices return.

wrong.why: one whole sounds like the number one
wrong.move: writes the number one on top when every slice is taken
wrong.screen: every slice is numbered in turn as it clicks into the box, the last number lands on the top box, and the card shows the same number above and below

phases.screen: a pizza cut into equal slices, every slice on the blue plate, an empty pizza box on the board and the card empty
phases.soWhat: when the top and bottom numbers are the same, every part is taken and the fraction is one whole
phases.concept: All the parts make one whole

phases.win: the card shows the stacked fraction and the words card names it, such as three-sevenths
phases.does: counts all the things on the shelf and in the basket, counts the things in the basket, types both, then reads the name in words
phases.goal: a group is counted like a whole: all the things go below the line and the things taken go above it

phases.check: Away from the screen: some of the children in the class are wearing blue. How would you write the fraction of the class that wears blue?
phases.feels: the same card that named part of a pizza naming part of a shelf of things
phases.hands: Line up a row of mangoes, laddoos or counters on the desk, move some of them into a bowl, and write how many are in the bowl above the line and how many there are in all below it.

phases.screen: Group view with a shelf of mangoes, some already in the blue basket, and an empty fraction card
phases.soWhat: all the things go below the line and the things taken go above it
phases.concept: A fraction of a group of things

writeup.delight: On the third phase, the last slice clicks into the pizza box and the pizza closes into one whole inside a green outline with no gap and no slice left on the plate, while the card still shows the same number above the line and below it. On the first phase the torn roti wobbles, and its pieces slide back to equal parts when the slider returns to the middle.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a chapati, a pizza and a cake stand on the shelf with their cuts drawn and nothing taken, the chosen whole on the amber board, the Cut dial set low, and the name card blank. On the second a chocolate bar, a jug of juice and a pizza wait on the shelf, the deep blue plate is empty, and the fraction card shows an empty line with two empty boxes. On the third a pizza is cut into slices that all lie on the blue plate, with an empty pizza box open on the board. On the fourth the Group view is on, with a shelf of separate mangoes, some already in the deep blue basket, and the card empty. One thing moves, once: the first cut line, or the first thing on the shelf on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any whole from the shelf cut into two to ten parts, taken any way, torn unevenly and put back together again, and the Group view with any shelf of things. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming equal parts, refusing a torn roti, writing a fraction from the parts taken, making one whole and counting a group, each on a real thing.
voiceLines: A kitchen table with a chapati, a pizza and a cake.
Cut the chapati into equal parts. What is one part called?
Take some pieces. Count the pieces you took, then count all the pieces.
Put the slices back in the box. What do they make?
Here is a group of things. Count them all, then count the ones in the basket.
A new whole. Look at the cuts first.
Free play. Cut, take and put back as you like.
Count the parts again, one cut line at a time.
You named every fraction by counting.

observations.why: a name like third means one of three parts that are all the same size.
observations.soWhat: the parts must be equal before a fraction can name them.
observations.observe: The torn roti made one piece bigger, and the words card would not name any piece.

observations.why: the whole was cut into the same number of parts every time.
observations.soWhat: the denominator counts all the equal parts, taken or not.
observations.observe: The bottom number stayed the same while more pieces went onto the blue plate.

observations.why: all the parts of a whole make that whole.
observations.soWhat: when the top and bottom numbers are the same, the fraction is one whole.
observations.observe: The last slice clicked into the pizza box and the pizza closed with no gap left.

observations.why: a group of separate things works like a whole cut into parts.
observations.soWhat: a fraction can name part of a group as well as part of a thing.
observations.observe: The same card named part of a pizza and part of a shelf of mangoes.

source_tool.description: A kitchen table fills the working area. A shelf of wholes runs across the top with a round chapati with toasted spots, a pizza with toppings, a round cake, a chocolate bar with its squares and a jug of juice with equal marks, and a torn roti at its far end. The child chooses one, and it comes down onto an amber board with a Cut dial under it that sets two to ten equal parts. The cut lines are drawn first in near-black, so the number of parts can be counted before anything is taken. Tapping a part lifts it onto a deep blue plate beside the board, where it keeps its natural colours, and tapping it again puts it back; parts that stay on the board are the ones left. A fraction card at the right is built by typing two numbers from the pad: the number of parts taken goes above a level line and the number of all the parts goes below it. The top box is labelled numerator and the bottom box denominator once the child has met them, and a words card under the card says the name aloud and in writing, such as one-third. An Uneven cut slider tears the roti, or moves one cut off the middle, on purpose, and the words card then refuses every fraction name and says that the parts are not equal. A Put together button clicks the slices back into the pizza box until it closes into one whole inside a green outline. A Shape view button redraws the same cut whole as a plain shape with the taken parts coloured deep blue. A Group view swaps the whole for a shelf of up to twenty separate real things, mangoes, laddoos, kites, balloons, bananas or bangles, each one tappable and lifted into a deep blue basket, so the same card names part of a group. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many parts are taken out of how many there are.
source_tool.art_direction: A kitchen table with real food / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a round chapati with its toasted spots, a pizza with toppings, a cake, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, laddoos, mangoes, bananas, kites, balloons, pencils, marbles, bangles, books. The object is the thing the child works on, and a plain shape appears only as a second view the child can switch to.
A part is never drawn without its whole. The whole object stays in the frame, entire, with the parts that were not taken still drawn and still countable.

Every division into parts is made by a drawn cut line, score line or gap, never by a change of colour alone, and the cuts go in before anything is taken, so the bottom number can be counted whether anything is taken or not.

Where a fraction says its parts are equal, every part is drawn the same size and the same shape. Where a stage deliberately shows unequal parts, such as a roti torn unevenly, it says so in its own label and no fraction name is written against them.

Taking a part is something the child does: a slice is lifted onto the deep blue plate, a mango is dropped into the deep blue basket. The plate and the basket carry the colour code, and the object keeps its own colours.
A fraction is always written with its top number above a level line and its bottom number below it, both upright and centred. The line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
Two like fractions are shown as two objects of the same size laid one under the other from one common left edge, so that the taken parts ending in different places carries the claim.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a part, a counter or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a chapati stays toasted brown and a mango stays yellow. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting the object. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of that same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every cut line, outline and plain edge is near-black, and a part of a drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its outline. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Coloured or Taken, Left, Whole and Bigger, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the parts again, one cut line at a time.
voice.onNext: A new whole. Look at the cuts first.
voice.opening: A kitchen table with a chapati, a pizza and a cake.
voice.onFinish: You named every fraction by counting.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Cut, take and put back as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Equal parts: halves, thirds and quarters
Coloured parts: the top and bottom numbers
All the parts make one whole
A fraction of a group of things

placement.where: After each child has cut a paper chapati or a paper plate pizza into equal parts and lifted some pieces onto a plate by hand, and before any fraction is written on the board. The tool is what lets an uneven cut be tried on purpose and refused on the spot, and what clicks the slices back into one whole again and again, which a cut paper cannot do twice.

answer_key.rule: A whole cut into equal parts gives fractions. Two equal parts are halves, three equal parts are thirds and four equal parts are fourths, or quarters. The parts must be equal, or there is no fraction to name them. The bottom number, the denominator, counts all the equal parts in the whole. The top number, the numerator, counts the parts that are coloured or taken. When the top and bottom numbers are the same, every part is taken and the fraction is one whole. A group works like a whole: the bottom number counts all the things and the top number counts the things taken.
answer_key.wrong: The object is shown again beside the writing and the two are counted together: the cuts first, then the taken parts, a small number lighting on each in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: All 3 slices are the same size, so the parts are equal.
One slice is one-third of the pizza.
items.question: A pizza is cut into 3 equal slices. What is one slice called?
items.checkpoint: The parts must be equal before they can be named.
items.misconception: Calling it a half, because half is the only part name the child knows.

steps: Count all the equal parts: 6. That is the bottom number, the denominator.
Count the parts taken: 4. That is the top number, the numerator.
Write 4 above the line and 6 below it.
items.question: A chocolate bar has 6 equal squares and 4 squares are taken. Write the fraction. Which number is the numerator?
items.checkpoint: The bottom number counts all the equal parts. The top number counts the parts taken.
items.misconception: Writing the six on top and the four below, so the fraction is upside down.

steps: The cake has 7 equal slices, so the bottom number is 7.
Every slice is taken, so the top number is 7.
The top and bottom numbers are the same, so the slices together make one whole cake.
items.question: A round cake is cut into 7 equal slices and every slice is on the plate. Write the fraction. What does it make?
items.checkpoint: When the top and bottom numbers are the same, the fraction is one whole.
items.misconception: Writing 1 on top and 7 below because one whole means the number one goes on top.

steps: Count all the laddoos: 10. That goes below the line.
Count the yellow laddoos: 6. That goes above the line.
Write 6 above 10, and say it as six-tenths.
items.question: A tray has 10 laddoos. 6 are yellow and the rest are orange. What fraction of the laddoos are yellow? Write it in numbers and in words.
items.checkpoint: In a group, all the things go below the line and the counted things go above it.
items.misconception: Writing the yellow laddoos over the orange ones, 6 over 4, instead of over all of the laddoos.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A chapati is cut into 2 equal parts. What is one part called?
A jug of juice has 7 equal marks, and the juice reaches 5 marks. What fraction of the jug is full?
A pizza is cut into thirds. How many thirds make the whole pizza?
A shelf holds 9 balloons and 7 of them are red. What fraction of the balloons are red?
A roti is torn into 3 pieces, but one piece is much bigger than the other two. Can the big piece be called one-third? Why?
items.final_answer: No. The 3 pieces are not equal, so none of them can be called a third

items.question: A chocolate bar has 5 equal squares, and all 5 squares are back in the wrapper. Write the missing top number: [ ]/5
A cake is cut into 8 equal slices and 1 slice is taken. Then 1 more slice is taken. Which number of the fraction changes, and what is the new fraction?
items.final_answer: The top number changes, from 1 to 2. The new fraction is 2/8

items.question: A box has 10 bangles and 3 of them are red. What fraction of the bangles are red, and what fraction are not red?
items.final_answer: 3/10 are red and 7/10 are not red

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: chooses the whole to work on: chapati, pizza, cake, chocolate bar, jug or the torn roti
cuts the whole into two to ten equal parts, the cut lines drawn first
lifts it onto the deep blue plate, or puts it back when tapped again
tears the roti or moves one cut off the middle, and the words card refuses every name
clicks the slices back into the pizza box one by one until it closes into one whole
redraws the same cut whole as a plain shape with the taken parts coloured deep blue
swaps the whole for a shelf of up to twenty separate real things that are lifted into the basket
types the top and bottom numbers of the fraction card

teaching_notes: Give each child a roti or a paper plate pizza to fold and cut before the tool opens, one into two parts, one into three and one into four, and ask them to say the name of one part aloud. Insist on equal parts and wait for a child to say why a torn roti cannot be named, rather than saying it for them. Always count the cuts before the parts taken, and say the bottom number first. Use a real row of mangoes, laddoos or counters for the Group view. If a child writes the taken count underneath, ask which number tells how many parts the whole was cut into. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's pictures are the child's to colour and write.
generation_prompt: Build a fractions tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, a kitchen table with real food drawn as recognisable flat illustrations in their natural colours. A shelf of wholes runs across the top of the working area: a round chapati with toasted spots, a pizza with toppings, a round cake, a chocolate bar with squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, and a torn roti. The chosen whole sits on an amber board at the left, and a Cut dial under it sets two to ten equal parts with the near-black cut lines drawn before anything is taken. Tapping a part lifts it onto a deep blue plate beside the board, and tapping it again puts it back. A fraction card at the right is built from the number pad: the parts taken above a level line, all the parts below it, the top box labelled numerator and the bottom box denominator once met. A words card names the fraction. An Uneven cut slider tears the roti or moves one cut off the middle and the words card refuses every name. A Put together button clicks the slices back into the pizza box one by one until it closes into one whole inside a green outline. A Shape view button redraws the cut whole as a plain shape with the taken parts deep blue. A Group view swaps the whole for a shelf of up to twenty separate real things, mangoes, laddoos, kites, balloons, bananas or bangles, each tappable and lifted into a deep blue basket. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the parts taken out of all the parts. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Pick a whole from the shelf. Cut it into equal parts. Lift some parts onto the blue plate. Count all the parts, then count the parts you took. Put the parts back together.
